evidence.title: Context-Aware Alerting in Elderly Care Facilities: A Hybrid Framework Integrating LLM Reasoning with Rule-Based Logic
evidence.outcome: Alarm load reduction to nurses by context-aware filtering versus notifying all nurses
evidence.effect: Average alarm load reduced to 27.5% (72.5% reduction) versus 100% baseline; macro F1 0.18 to 0.97; FPR 0.20 to 0.005; FNR 0.79 to 0.023.
evidence.quote: Compared to the baseline where all nurses were notified (100% alarm load), the proposed method reduced average alarm load to 27.5%, achieving a 72.5% reduction, with suppression rates reaching 100% in some rooms for some nurses.
evidence.sample_unit: elderly residents (with four nurses, three rooms, seven days)

evidence.title: OB HUB: Remote Electronic Fetal Monitoring Surveillance
evidence.venue: MCN. The American journal of maternal child nursing
evidence.outcome: Neonatal outcomes and perceived safety with remote nurse AI-assisted fetal surveillance
evidence.effect: Cooling 6 (0.25%) pre vs 2 (0.08%) during trial, p = .10; no significant differences in neonatal outcomes; 78.8% of responding nurses said OB HUB improved safety.
evidence.quote: There were no significant differences between groups for neonatal outcomes.

evidence.title: Real-World Evaluation of a Remote Patient Monitoring Service for Early Detection of Clinical Deterioration in Skilled Nursing Facilities
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Directors Association
evidence.outcome: Alert burden and predictive value of AI alerts reviewed by remote clinical team before on-site staff
evidence.effect: Remote team review preceded alerts to on-site staff; overall PPV 35.4%; 23.9 unique patients alerted per 100 beds per month, described as manageable alert burden.
evidence.quote: RPM using continuous, contactless cardiorespiratory monitoring enabled early identification of certain patient deterioration events with clinically meaningful sensitivity and lead time, and manageable alert burden, complementing standard care.
evidence.sample_unit: unplanned potentially preventable hospital transfers (across 184 SNFs)

evidence.title: Randomized Controlled Trial to Assess the Feasibility of a Novel Clinical Decision Support System Based on the Automatic Generation of Alerts through Remote Patient Monitoring
evidence.outcome: Alert burden on healthcare professionals from high-volume remote monitoring alerts
evidence.effect: Case group generated far more alerts (61,827 vs. 1825; p < 0.05) but without overloading healthcare professionals thanks to automatic AI alert management.
evidence.quote: The case group received a more exhaustive follow-up, with a higher number of alerts (61,827 vs. 1825; p < 0.05) but without overloading healthcare professionals thanks to automatic alert management through artificial intelligence.

evidence.title: Don’t set and forget: Optimising Digital Early Warning Tools through upgrade and evaluation
evidence.effect: Focus groups and surveys identified alert fatigue; its frequency and severity were not quantified.
evidence.quote: Stakeholder focus groups and surveys identified a lack of awareness of specific functionality, issues with alert fatigue, technical challenges with the system, the need for training and concerns around over-reliance on the system by junior staff.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-powered tiered early warning framework addressing high false alarm rates for in-hospital mortality prediction
evidence.outcome: False alarm burden (low PPV) from single-threshold IHM alerts
evidence.effect: At Youden thresholds PPVs were 13.9% in H1, 11.0% in H2, 9.8% in H3, implying most alerts are false positives.
evidence.quote: However, PPVs remained low (13.9% in H1, 11.0% in H2, and 9.8% in H3), revealing a high false positive burden under realistic deployment conditions.

commentary.bottom_line: Three studies test some form of filtering alerts before they reach frontline staff, and only one, a retrospective analysis across 184 skilled nursing facilities, examines a remote clinical review team, reporting a positive predictive value of 35.4%. No study compares remote nurse review against direct alerting on alert fatigue or patient outcomes, so support for this practice rests on thin evidence.

perspectives.view: The one comparative test enrolled 28 residents over seven days and evaluated automated context-aware filtering rather than a nurse team, which makes it indirect. The other two tests lack a concurrent comparator. Imprecision, indirectness, and design limits place certainty for remote nurse review at very low.

In remote fetal surveillance, therapeutic cooling went from 6 (0.25%) to 2 (0.08%) cases, p = .10, with no significant differences in neonatal outcomes. These data do not show whether remote review catches deterioration earlier. Reported PPVs of 9.8% to 13.9% for single-threshold alerts suggest a filtering layer has many false alarms to remove.

Across 184 skilled nursing facilities, remote team review preceded on-site alerts and yielded 23.9 unique patients alerted per 100 beds per month, which authors described as manageable. A Spanish trial reported that automatic AI alert management handled 61,827 alerts without overloading staff, which suggests automated filtering may serve as an alternative to a human review layer.

Two of the three tests enrolled older adults in nursing homes or skilled nursing facilities, and none reported Medicaid status, safety-net setting, preferred language, or literacy. Whether remote review performs equally for these groups has not been examined.

The practice requires a staffed remote nurse team, and no study reports its cost, staffing ratio, or reviewer workload. In the fetal surveillance program, 78.8% of responding nurses said the remote hub improved safety, which suggests staff acceptance but does not measure efficiency or return on investment.

commentary.research_gap: No study randomizes or concurrently compares routing AI early-warning alerts through a remote nurse team with sending them directly to frontline clinicians. Such a study would measure alert fatigue, time to clinical response, patient outcomes, and staffing cost, and it would also compare remote human review with automated alert filtering.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the three tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two studied older adults in residential or skilled nursing care, and the third described its sample only as births. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume the reported alert burden or acceptance figures will apply to their patients.
